title: God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen
origin: Traditional English carol; the minor-mode 'London' tune, first printed by William Sandys in 1833

pd.detail: Anonymous English carol in circulation well before 1900; the London tune is associated with the dance air 'Chestnut, or Dove's Figary' in Playford's The English Dancing Master (1651) and was first printed with this text by William Sandys, Christmas Carols Ancient and Modern, London, 1833.
pd.sourceEdition: The London tune as printed in 'The Everyday Song Book' (1927), four-part setting in E minor, verified note for note and rhythm for rhythm; melodic outline independently confirmed against the Hymnary.org incipit for the tune GOD REST YOU MERRY (11554 32171 23451), which matches the encoded verse exactly.
pd.notes: Melody and harmony only; no lyrics are carried. This is the traditional minor-mode London tune, not any modern rock or orchestral arrangement of it. Meter was checked before encoding: both consulted transcriptions notate the carol in 4/4 with four even quarter-note beats to the bar, so nothing is forced here -- this is not one of the 3/4 or 6/8 carols. The tune is genuinely Aeolian: deg 7 (D natural) is never raised to a leading tone even where the harmonisation uses B7, so the validator's minor-key leading-tone warning is expected and correct here. The tune has a one-beat pickup; per the song book pickup rule it is carried on the last beat of whichever section precedes, so the two-bar intro sets up verse-a and the chorus sets up the next verse. Verse A, Verse B, Verse C and the Chorus are the source's own four lines, encoded note for note; the Chorus's last bar is a rest plus the pickup into the next verse, added so the section is a whole 8 bars. The two-bar Intro is editorial: it is the chorus's own closing descent (5-4-3-2 / held 1) used as a lead-in, not extra tune.

pd.detail: Anonymous English carol text with no identified author at any stage of its transmission: attested in a manuscript of the early 1650s, printed on a broadsheet of about 1760, and referred to in the Monthly Review of November 1764, so it was in wide circulation long before 1900.
pd.sourceEdition: William Sandys, Christmas Carols Ancient and Modern (London: Richard Beckley, 1833), pp. 102-104 -- his stanzas 1 and 3 and his own two-line refrain, transcribed line by line from that printing (spelling and capitalisation as printed) rather than from modern singing practice.

lyrics.notes: The A phrase, first couplet of the stanza. Sandys prints seven stanzas (verified page by page against the 1833 setting, pp. 102-104); two are carried here -- his 1 and 3, the opening and the angel-and-shepherds stanza most often sung second -- and the rest are omitted purely for length. Nothing in this carol is offensive and no verse is dropped on those grounds. The whole text comes from that single 1833 printing rather than mixed across editions, so Sandys's readings stand wherever they differ from the c.1760 broadside or from modern singing practice. Line 1 is pinned to bar 0 and sung from the one-beat pickup carried at the end of the preceding section; line 2 is pinned to bar 2, the downbeat its phrase lands on, with the low deg-7 at beat 7 as its anacrusis -- the same convention the other lyric songs in this book use, where a pickup is charted with the bar its phrase occupies. Both stanzas are sung by the shipped form: the second pass opens with a Verse 2a Part so the second stanza is complete rather than starting mid-sentence.

lyrics.notes: The repeat of the A phrase, second couplet of the stanza. Same two-bar line pacing as verse-a: line 1 pinned to bar 0 off the pickup carried at the end of the previous section, line 2 pinned to bar 2 with the beat-7 anacrusis belonging to it. AUDIT NOTE: stanza 1 line 2 was corrected here to Sandys's own 1833 stanza reading; the wording that had been encoded is the modern standardised one, which Sandys uses only in his refrain, not in the stanza. The two are near-identical in sense but not word for word, and the difference is in the source, so the chorus and this section deliberately do not match.

lyrics.notes: The B phrase, third and last couplet of the stanza. This is the eight-syllable line of the verse, which is why the tune climbs from deg 6 up to the octave across bars 0-1 before the answering line falls back; line 1 is pinned to bar 0 and line 2 to bar 2.

stanzas.text: To save us all from Satan's power
How that in Bethlehem was born
The Son of God by name.

pd.sourceEdition: William Sandys, Christmas Carols Ancient and Modern (London: Richard Beckley, 1833), pp. 102-104 -- his stanzas 1 and 3 and his own two-line refrain, transcribed line by line from that printing (spelling and capitalisation as printed) rather than from modern singing practice.

lyrics.notes: IMPORTANT -- this is the SANDYS 1833 refrain, printed there as two lines and lineated here as three so it sits on the tune's three phrases. It is NOT the doubled 'comfort and joy' refrain everyone sings: that shape became standard through Carols for Choirs (1961), whereas Sandys writes his refrain out once after stanza 1 and abbreviates it after every later stanza. Sandys's refrain does restate the stanza's second couplet, but with its own closing wording, which is not identical to his stanza 1 wording; both are transcribed exactly as printed, so verse-b and this section are deliberately not word for word. One stanza only: the refrain is the same after every verse, so both Chorus Parts sing it. Bar alignment against the encoded head: line 1 over bars 0-1, line 2 over bars 2-3, line 3 over the rising bars 4-6 with its last syllable on the four-beat deg-1 in bar 6. Bar 7 is a rest plus the pickup into the next verse and carries no words.

stanzas.text: O tidings of comfort and joy,
